adrs.title: Use a CRDT (Yjs) first, not OT
adrs.consequence: Offline editing is nearly free, but a document never shrinks back to just its text.

c.v: Two families of algorithm solve live collaboration. One sends every edit to a central server that rewrites it against everything the sender had not seen yet. The other gives every character a permanent identity, so edits merge in any order, on any copy, with no referee.

We took the second, reusing a proven implementation of the data structure and writing the network, server, presence and persistence around it by hand. The merging is the subtle part, and reusing it removes a whole class of bugs we would otherwise have written ourselves.

The payoff is that the server relays bytes it never has to understand, which is what makes working offline cheap. The price is size: deleted characters leave markers behind, so a document costs more than the words in it and never gets smaller again.
The other approach was built later, as a second engine to compare against rather than to ship. Writing it first would have spent the entire budget on getting one transform right.

adrs.title: Isolate concurrency control behind an engine interface
adrs.consequence: Nothing above the engine layer knows which algorithm runs underneath, and a test enforces it.

c.v: The goal is to run both algorithms and compare them. They need different things from a server: one can broadcast and forget, the other must hold the authoritative document and answer the sender as well as everyone else. Assume the first shape everywhere and adding the second stops being a feature and becomes a rewrite.

So there is one interface on each side — one on the server, one in the editor — and the engine sits behind it. Everything above it is written once: the editor, formatting, cursors, comments, storage and the API. The only freedom the interface grants is deciding who a reply goes to.

Three rules keep it honest. Nothing above the line names a specific engine, storage keeps sealed bytes it never interprets, and cursors are handled by the transport rather than the engine so they behave identically under both.
Adding the second engine should therefore touch the engine and almost nothing else. If transport, storage or presence needed changes, the seam leaked. ADR-004 reports how it went.

adrs.title: Append-only update log plus periodic snapshots
adrs.consequence: Kill the server mid-sentence, start it again, and nothing that was typed is lost.

c.v: Every keystroke produces a change. Rewriting the whole document for each one costs more the longer the document gets, and makes storage the bottleneck long before the network is.

So changes are appended to a log and never rewritten, which keeps a write the same cost forever. Every so often the log is folded into a snapshot of the document as it stood, so opening it later means reading one snapshot and a short tail instead of replaying an entire history.

Writes never wait for a merge, so a keystroke is acknowledged immediately, and recovery after a crash is just replaying that tail. Folding has to be all-or-nothing, or a crash in the middle of it loses edits.

Storage never learns what any of the bytes mean, which is what lets both engines share it. Snapshots hold the whole document, so a very large one makes folding expensive — a later problem, not this one.

adrs.title: OT engine — server authority and bounded history
adrs.consequence: Server authority is real: work done while offline is discarded on reconnect.

c.v: An edit here describes a walk across the whole document rather than a position and some text. Positional edits cannot be combined with one another, and combining them is exactly what keeps a slow link from building an unbounded backlog of typing.

The server decides the order. When two edits collide it always resolves them the same way round, identically on every copy — that is the concrete meaning of "server-authoritative". Each client keeps exactly one edit in flight, which bounds how much history the server has to rewrite for anybody.

History is finite, so a client returning after too long cannot be caught up. It is sent the current document and loses its unsent work, rather than silently corrupting the shared one. That is the honest cost of this design, and the reason the product does not use it.
The transform is checked against thousands of randomly generated documents on every build, and the generator is seeded so any failure can be replayed exactly.

adrs.title: Network simulation by socket substitution
adrs.consequence: The lab can cut one replica off the network without a line of sync code knowing.

c.v: The lab needs to slow, drop and black-hole traffic for one client at a time, and to show every frame going in both directions. The question is where that hooks in.

It hooks in at the connection. The lab hands the sync layer something that behaves exactly like a real connection and is not one, so nothing above it changes and no engine code is aware. This is the payoff of writing the transport by hand — you cannot instrument a dependency you do not own.

Three limits are deliberate. Frames are never reordered, because a real connection does not do that and faking it would break a client for a reason that cannot happen. Dropped frames are labelled a thought experiment. And a partition is silent: the connection stays open, nothing crosses, no error fires, which is nastier than pulling the cable.

Defects that no amount of green testing reaches become reproducible, because the lab can create the condition rather than wait for it. Under a two-second link, a burst of typing reaches the other replica in about 2.3 seconds with the CRDT and about 6.1 with OT, where one edit in flight costs two round trips.

adrs.title: Rich text — formatting as an ordinary edit
adrs.consequence: Formatting rides on an ordinary edit, which saved nine collision cases in the transform.

c.v: Rich text over a tree structure is a research project. Over a flat sequence of characters it is not, and this is meant to be an editor somebody would actually write in, which plain text is not.

So bolding is expressed as "move across five characters and change how they look". It neither inserts nor deletes, so the length arithmetic underneath is untouched — a dedicated formatting edit would have added nine new collision cases instead of none. Line-level formatting rides on the newline that ends the line, which keeps the document flat rather than a tree.

Formatting is nearly free under the CRDT, where it lives on the character itself, and costs real work under the other engine, which has to carry it through every collision. Concurrent bold and un-bold is a tie with no plain-text equivalent: both sides agree on the letters and disagree on the look.

Randomised testing found two bugs within a few hundred runs that no hand-written test would have. Both left documents that still looked right, which is why the checks compare whole documents rather than the visible text.

adrs.title: Accounts, ownership and per-document roles
adrs.consequence: Roles are enforced on the connection, where the interface cannot be talked out of them.

c.v: A client used to name itself and be believed. Making documents owned forces a question the project had not had to answer: what a client is allowed to do, as distinct from what it is able to send.

People are stored apart from documents, in one place both engine servers share. A document belongs to an engine because only that engine can read its history; a person does not. A document has one owner and gives everyone else a role, editor or viewer — two roles, because two are all the server actually enforces.

Whether you may open a document is answered once, before the connection is accepted. Whether you may change it is answered on every edit, because only the engine can tell an edit from a greeting. Sessions travel in an explicit header rather than a cookie, since a browser attaches cookies by itself, including on requests coming from other sites.

The two engines refuse a forbidden edit differently, so the editor is made genuinely read-only rather than left to fail quietly. The assertions that matter are the negative ones: a viewer's edit is rejected by the server, and revoking access disconnects someone already connected.

adrs.title: Version history — retention, checkpoints, and restore as an edit
adrs.consequence: Restoring is an ordinary edit, so a restore can itself be undone.

c.v: History is only free if folding the log keeps what it folds. Folding old changes into a snapshot and throwing them away leaves anything older than that with no recoverable past at all.

So folding archives instead of deleting, and the archive and the live log concatenate back into one ordered history. Each fold also leaves a checkpoint behind for free, so rebuilding an old version is the nearest checkpoint plus a short replay, and naming a version is just labelling one of them.

Restoring appends the old text as a new edit rather than rewinding. Rewinding would destroy every version after the one restored, and restoring is the thing people do by accident. Under the CRDT the old characters are still there underneath, which is what lets a restore merge with someone else's concurrent typing instead of clobbering it.
Archived history ages out on a schedule, with checkpoints and the changes they need pruned in step so no version is offered that cannot be rebuilt. Named checkpoints are kept for good.

adrs.title: CRDT for the product, OT for the lab
adrs.consequence: The product is CRDT-only; the choice moved to the lab, where it is shown rather than asked.

c.v: Offering both engines everywhere makes somebody choose a concurrency algorithm before they can write anything down — with real consequences, since under one of them work done offline is discarded — and with nothing in the product to judge the choice against. Two buttons teach nobody the difference; they only ask.
So every document on the site is a CRDT. No engine picker and no engine badge, which with one engine would label every row identically.
The other engine stays, whole: the engine, the shared transform and every property test, with its server still running. The seam is only real while a second implementation keeps it honest.

The lab is where the engine is a choice, next to the machinery that makes the comparison legible — real replicas, injectable partitions and a decoded timeline. The price is that a document made on one engine does not exist on the other, which is cheaper than asking a writer to pick an algorithm.

adrs.title: Anyone may write, only an account may share
adrs.consequence: A document made without an account is open to anyone holding the link.

c.v: Giving documents owners implied a rule nobody actually decided: sign up before you can write anything. Meanwhile the thing that genuinely needs an account — sharing — could only say "the owner may share", which on a document with no owner is true and useless.
Creating and editing need no account. The document is simply unowned, which was already a state the system understood, so nothing new had to be invented beside it.

Sharing needs an account, because of what sharing is: granting access writes down a person, so there has to be a person at both ends. That is the one place in the product where the sign-in wall stands.

Claiming is the bridge, walked in place — sign in, claim, share — and it costs something that is said out loud. Anyone else editing anonymously is disconnected when a document gains an owner, and the message names the reason. Documents made without an account are remembered on the device, as a convenience list rather than a record of who may open them.

adrs.title: Attributes that carry values, and the boundary they need
adrs.consequence: A collaborator's formatting value is untrusted input and meets an allowlist before it reaches the page.

c.v: Growing eight on-or-off marks into a word-processor toolbar needs no change to the machinery underneath, which does not care what the marks are called. What had to be decided is what the new ones are.

There turn out to be three kinds: flags like bold, values like colour, size, font and links, and line-level ones like headings and alignment. Only the middle kind becomes styling or a link on the page, and it is written by whoever is editing and arrives over the network — which makes it untrusted input.

So exactly one place turns a value into something the page renders, and it checks against a list of what is allowed rather than trying to neutralise what is not. A refused value drops the formatting and keeps the words. The check lives at the point of rendering, not the point of typing, because an attacker need not use the typing path at all.

Bulleted and numbered are one setting with two values, not two independent switches, so a line can never claim to be both. The number on an ordered list is worked out from the lines above rather than stored, since storing it would make every insertion rewrite the document.

adrs.title: Comment anchors — relative under CRDT, server-authoritative under OT
adrs.consequence: Measured: anchors converge under insertion and diverge under deletion.

c.v: A comment is attached to a range of text. Between writing it and reading it, other people insert and delete around and inside that range, and it has to still be about the same words.

Under the CRDT an anchor names a character and the character carries it, so there is nothing to keep in step. Under the other engine the server owns anchors: it already decides the order everything happens in, so it moves every anchor once in that order — convergence from authority rather than from the algorithm.

That holds for insertions and fails for deletions, and the failure was measured rather than assumed. Deleting text that straddles an anchor destroys the characters that located it, so two copies applying the same pair of changes in opposite orders can legally land it in different places. Thousands of concurrent insertions converge; one pinned counterexample shows the same thing breaking the moment a delete is allowed.

Deleting every commented character orphans the comment rather than reattaching it to text it was never about. The counterexample is pinned rather than described, so nobody later "fixes" the divergence by quietly weakening the test.

adrs.title: Images and tables, without introducing a tree
adrs.consequence: Neither engine changed at all, and no table-aware merge code exists anywhere.

c.v: The obvious way to add images and tables is a tree. Once the document is a tree, every edit needs a path rather than a position and merging has to handle nodes moving between parents — a research problem, for a feature that has nothing to do with concurrency.

So an image is a single character that happens to carry a picture. It has one position, so an insertion shifts it, a deletion removes it, a comment can already point at it, and two people adding one at the same spot are already ordered. The cost is that an image can be replaced but not edited.

A table is a run of lines with a separator character between cells. Text inside a cell is ordinary document text, so two people typing in different cells are just two people typing in one line. Merged cells, column widths and nested tables are out, because each one smuggles the tree back in.

Nothing in either engine changed; the work is all in how the document is drawn. It is asserted against both engines: an image survives concurrent editing around it, and two clients typing in different cells converge. Pictures must be linked rather than embedded, or every copy of the document would carry them forever.

adrs.title: A tab is a document
adrs.consequence: A tab gets its own room, history and comments; sharing is inherited from the document.

c.v: Tabs are several independent bodies of text sharing one title, one owner and one access list. A document here is already a precise thing, so the only real question is where the seam goes.

Putting several texts inside one engine fails three ways: unrelated texts would share one revision line, everything keyed by document would need re-plumbing, and opening one tab would load all of them. So a tab is simply a document of its own, with a name that says which document it belongs to.

Access is inherited, never copied. A per-tab copy of the permissions is a second version of the truth, and its failure mode is a collaborator who can read four tabs and not the fifth. A document with no tabs is one tab; adding a second names the first rather than moving it, since moving it would rewrite a history and orphan every comment.

Comments and history follow the tab, while the title, sharing and the task list follow the document. Which tab you are looking at is your own view rather than everyone's — a shared selection would yank other people's screens. Cursors are per tab, so two people in different tabs are not editing the same text.

adrs.title: The task list is not a document
adrs.consequence: Deliberately not a CRDT — and the argument for why that instinct is wrong.

c.v: In a project built around CRDTs the instinct is to reach for the CRDT again, and saying why that is wrong is the only interesting part of this decision.

Concurrent editing is expensive because two people change the same sequence at overlapping positions and both changes have to survive. A checklist has none of that shape: two additions are two rows, two ticks agree about the outcome, a reword is last-writer-wins on a short string, and a deletion done twice is a deletion. The only field two people race on is a checkbox, and when they race they agree.

So tasks are rows, not text: changed and read over ordinary requests, with no anchor into the document, because a task is about the document rather than about a range inside it. Ticking is instant in the interface and confirmed by the server, since a checkbox that waits for a round trip reads as broken.

The list belongs to the document rather than to a tab, and it behaves identically under both engines with no engine-specific code — the claim being tested is that there is no difference to hide. Tasks are not versioned: restoring yesterday's prose should not roll back what is still to do.

adrs.title: Batch broadcasts in a window, and let the engine decide
adrs.consequence: Messages drop 24x in a busy room; bytes barely move, because the bytes are the edits.

c.v: Relaying one person's keystroke to everyone else in the room means traffic in a document grows with the square of the people in it. This is the first thing in the system to break.

So outgoing changes are held for a fiftieth of a second, merged into one, and sent once to the whole room. The engine has to allow it, and only the CRDT can: its changes merge by construction, and applying one twice does nothing.

Measured with everyone typing, the number of messages collapses — about 25 times fewer at a hundred editors — while the bytes fall by only about a third. Every client genuinely needs every edit and no window makes an edit smaller, so the quadratic cost never went away. What batching buys is paying it in bytes rather than in messages, and a message is the expensive unit.

Below five people in a room batching is a loss, because the merged message goes to everyone including whoever sent it, so it is switched off there — a threshold read off the measurements rather than picked. The delay it adds stays under the point where a remote cursor stops feeling live.

adrs.title: Search reads a projection, not the log
adrs.consequence: One index serves both engines, and it may be a couple of seconds behind.

c.v: "Which of my documents mentions the aqueduct at Segovia" had no answer at either end of the system. The client has never seen a document it is not open on, and the server stores every document in full without being able to read a word of it — which is exactly why storage survived a second engine untouched.

So search reads the plain text through the one part of the engine interface that speaks content, and keeps its own index beside the documents. The index is derived: it is authoritative about nothing, and dropping it loses nothing.

Re-reading a document cannot sit on the path of every keystroke, so indexing lags behind typing by a short pause. The cost is stated rather than hidden: a search may miss the last couple of seconds of writing.

A query is words, not a query language. Input is split on punctuation and each word treated literally, so a title with brackets in it is not a syntax error and a capitalised word never quietly means something. Results are limited to what you are allowed to open.

adrs.title: Authorship is free under the CRDT and built by hand under OT
adrs.consequence: The second asymmetry between the engines, and the first that favours the CRDT.

c.v: The CRDT already knows who wrote each character. Identity is not information bolted on afterwards — it is the mechanism that puts the characters in order in the first place.
The other engine structurally does not. It rewrites an incoming edit, applies it and records the result; what survives is text, and the record of who typed it never existed.

Both were built anyway, and the difference in what it cost is the finding. On one side, reading what is already there, including for documents written before the feature existed. On the other, a second record of one author per character, kept in step by hand with every edit and against the rewritten version of it, not the one the client sent.

Names are the sharper edge. The CRDT keeps identity inside the document, so it merges like the text; the other engine has to learn names from whoever is connected, so after a restart with nobody present the runs are right and the names are gone. A document it wrote before this existed is unattributable, permanently.

adrs.title: Postgres is the source of truth; anything in front of it is a cache
adrs.consequence: Nothing durable lives on the local disk, so a deploy that wipes it loses nothing.

c.v: The host throws its filesystem away on every deploy and every restart. A document's history is the document, so anything durable kept there is destroyed each time. A persistent disk is the host's own answer to that, and it pins the service to a single machine.

So one database holds everything durable, keeping each engine's documents and the shared list of people separated as before. There is no quiet fallback to a local file: a server that degraded to the disk when it could not reach the database would lose every document at the next restart, so it refuses to start instead.

A keystroke is no longer a free write — it crosses a network — so writes are gathered into a short window before being sent. That is a real reduction in durability, bounded, configurable, and turned off entirely wherever a test asserts on what was written.

Everything in front of the database may be lost: cursors, fan-out, the list of open rooms, the write buffer. A change is durable when the database has it, and nothing else is allowed to claim otherwise.

adrs.title: Signing in with Google
adrs.consequence: Identity is federated; authority is not.

c.v: Accounts asked a visitor who only wants to look at a collaborative editor to invent a password first. Adding a second way to sign in raises a question the project had not had to answer: what a credential is, as distinct from a person.

A credential belongs to a provider; a person does not. Sign-in methods are stored separately from people, keyed on the identifier the provider promises is stable rather than on an email address, which can change hands. A person may have a password, a provider, or both.

The provider's token is verified here and exchanged for one of our own sessions, so nothing downstream — sharing, ownership, the roles enforced on the connection — can tell a federated sign-in from a password one. Only identity is taken: signing in gives this application no access to anything else of yours.

Accounts are linked by email only when the provider says the address is verified, which is what makes it safe. Signing in with a password to an account that has none is refused exactly as an unknown address is, so nothing leaks about which addresses exist here. Leave it unconfigured and the feature is off rather than broken.

adrs.title: Importing a document from Drive
adrs.consequence: An import produces an independent document, and whatever will not fit is reported.

c.v: A document can be brought in from Drive, and the question that matters is whether it stays connected to the original. It cannot, sensibly: a two-way bridge means two concurrency systems arbitrating one document, with one of them winning, which inverts the thesis of this project.

So it is an import, not a sync. The file is exported once, converted into this editor's own formatting, and becomes an ordinary document here. There is no link back and the original is never written to.

Only the files you hand over are read, never everything you own, and nothing is kept afterwards that would let this application read your Drive while you are away. The whole job finishes in seconds, while you watch — so it needs no standing permission and involves no server of ours at all.

What will not survive the conversion is counted and named rather than quietly dropped. Tables become paragraphs: the grid is lost, the words are not. Pictures stay hosted where they were, which means they can stop resolving later, and that is reported too rather than fixed by copying them into the document forever.

adrs.title: Boot maintenance runs after the port opens
adrs.consequence: The first visit waits for a container to start, and for nothing else.

c.v: The site is slow on the first visit after a quiet period, and the obvious suspect is the database. Two measurements say otherwise.
The two suspensions are not the same size. The database wakes in a few hundred milliseconds; the machine hosting the site takes tens of seconds. The database was under one percent of the wait.

A cache could not have helped either, because the wait was housekeeping done before the site started answering at all — and a cache of the database cannot tell you which rows the database is missing. None of that work is needed to serve a request, so it now runs after the door is open, and a scheduled ping keeps the machine awake, which keeps the database warm as a side effect.

Housekeeping can therefore be interrupted, so a document may go unindexed across a boot that was cut short. Every task is safe to run again and does so next time, which is why it is allowed to fail without taking the server down.

adrs.title: Redis is optional, and rate limiting comes first
adrs.consequence: An unauthenticated request can no longer buy a tenth of a second of this server's only thread.

c.v: Checking a password is deliberately slow — about a tenth of a second of work — because that is what makes guessing at a stolen copy of it expensive. But this server has one thread and signing in needs no account, so the same property turns a cheap request into a tenth of a second of blocked server. A few hundred a second and it answers nothing at all, including the connections carrying every open document.
So requests are counted and limited centrally, before they reach anything, in four tiers. Centrally, because a limit each route has to remember to apply is one that a new route will forget.

rows.v: login, signup, signing in with a provider

c.v: Counting is per address, never per account: counting sign-in attempts per email would hand anyone a way to lock a specific person out of their own account. New connections are counted before they are accepted, because opening an unknown document creates it.

Redis is optional and its absence is a supported configuration, not a degraded one — on a single machine, counting in memory is faster. What Redis buys is counters that survive a restart, since a limit held in memory hands an attacker a fresh allowance for waiting.
